author: reek
body: The repository contains facts. Every fact is immutable, content- addressed, attributed, and typed. A "new version" of a definition is a new fact that supersedes an old fact. The old fact still exists. The repository is an append-only log.

author: reek
body: A proposal is a definition plus a justification plus a set of required stakeholders. There are no pull requests -- there are proposals.

author: reek
body: SignedFact, and the content a signature covers, are defined by Foreword chapter ImportGate -- the compiler cannot cite this chapter, and it must be able to check a signature. All that belongs here is the convenience of signing one with a Keypair, which is a Works notion.

author: reek
body: H7: a proposal as it travels the trust grid. The SignedAnnotation is the load-bearing carrier (the body holds the prose; this record adds the code suggestion, target chapter, and a stable timestamp). The outbox is a list of these on RepoState; the transport adapter drains it via TrustTransport.

author: reek
body: publish-verdict-accept is the path Damian named -- "boom i build, test, and publish the update on the spot". The gates (sweep / pingpong / verifier) run in the driver effect, not here.

author: reek
body: The verified flag on SignedAnnotation never travels -- it is receiver-local and recomputed via verify-annotation against the receiver's keyring.

author: reek
body: D.5: when a new annotation supersedes an old one (same kind, same target, but the new one wins by the resolution rule), the old hash is mapped to the new in the supersession HAMT. The Reader's default queries hide superseded entries.

author: reek
body: A repository depends on a definition from another repository by naming its content hash, never its name or its location. Two repositories that hold the same definition hold the same hash, so a dependency is the same dependency wherever it came from.

author: reek
body: Publishing a fact records it in the store and files its signature beside it. Importing one walks four guards -- present, hash-honest, signed by a key we hold, signed by someone we trust -- and any guard that fails refuses the import outright.

author: reek
body: The guards themselves are not here. They are in Foreword chapter ImportGate, because the compiler must one day run them and the compiler cannot cite this chapter. What is here is the half that is ours: the keyring, the vouch lattice, and the store the facts sit in. We do the expensive thinking and hand the gate a flat answer.

author: reek
body: The guard that matters is the last one. Trust was recorded long before it was enforced: the keyring has always carried a weight per key, and nothing anywhere refused a definition for falling below it. A fact one notch under the threshold now fails to import.

author: reek
body: What is gated is an importer. Nothing in the compile path calls repo-import yet -- there is no import directive in the language and no view that declares a threshold -- so a program that chooses to import is held to its threshold, and a build is not. Lifting the guards into the foreword is the first step of that reach; it is not yet the reach.

author: reek
body: The bridge between the lattice and the gate. The gate reads scores out of a flat manifest; the lattice computes them by walking a vouch graph. So we build the manifest the gate needs, for exactly the one signer it is about to ask about -- the signer named by the SignedFact filed under the hash we were handed.

author: reek
body: Building it for one signer rather than for the whole keyring is not only cheaper, it is the only thing available: a Keyring is a HAMT and a HAMT cannot be enumerated (keyring-scan-name is a stub returning None for exactly this reason). It also keeps the cost of an import where it was -- one vouch walk, for one key -- instead of one per key we hold.

author: reek
body: An empty manifest is the right answer whenever there is nobody to score: no fact, no signature, or a signer we hold no key for. The gate turns each of those into its own refusal.
